howItWorks.intro: A dollar figure that stays flat on paper can still lose a third of its punch in a decade, and that gap between what you see in your bank app and what it actually buys is the entire point of this tool. Enter your current savings, your annual income, an expected inflation rate, an expected annual raise, and a monthly savings contribution, and the calculator runs two separate erosion tracks side by side rather than a single generic "future value" number. The first track discounts your current savings balance at 1, 5, 10, and 20 years using Real Purchasing Power = Nominal Value ÷ (1 + Inflation Rate)^Years — the standard present-value-of-future-money formula economists use to strip inflation out of a dollar figure. The second track compares your income's growth path against inflation's growth path: your Income Gap is what you'd need to earn at year 10 just to maintain today's standard of living, minus what your stated annual raise actually gets you there. If your raise rate is lower than your inflation rate — a 3% raise against 4% inflation, for instance — that gap is negative and widens every year, because raises compound on top of last year's already-inflated number while your buying power compounds downward at the same time. A quick mental-math trick worth knowing: the Rule of 72 says you can estimate how long prices take to double by dividing 72 by the inflation rate. At 3% inflation, 72 ÷ 3 = 24 years for prices to double, which means purchasing power roughly halves over that same span — a useful sanity check against the calculator's exact exponential output. Worked example: $10,000 held today at a steady 3% average annual inflation rate is worth 10,000 ÷ (1.03)^20 ≈ 10,000 ÷ 1.8061 ≈ $5,537 in today's purchasing terms after 20 years — a loss of roughly $4,463, or about 44.6% of its original buying power, even though the number printed on the statement never changed. That's not a market crash or a bad investment; it's what happens to cash that just sits still while prices march upward year after year. The Total Wealth Erosion figure applies this same discounting to your ending balance after accounting for your monthly contributions, so you can see how much new saving is offsetting the old erosion versus how much ground you're still losing net.
rules: Real Purchasing Power = Nominal Value / (1 + Inflation Rate)^Years
Income Gap = Income Needed (inflation-adjusted) - Projected Income (raise-adjusted)
Total Erosion = Nominal Savings - Real Purchasing Power
howItWorks.outro: Two assumptions drive every number this calculator produces, so treat them as levers rather than facts: the inflation rate and the raise rate. Both are averages over a multi-year window, and real life is lumpier than that — the 2021-2023 stretch saw U.S. annual inflation run well above the 2% target the Federal Reserve typically aims for, driven by a mix of pandemic-era supply disruptions, stimulus spending, and energy price swings, before cooling back down as rate hikes took hold. A calculator built on a flat 3% assumption will understate erosion during a spike year and overstate it during a calm one, which is exactly why it's worth re-running this page with a higher rate (5-6%) and a lower one (1-2%) to see the spread rather than anchoring on a single output. It's also worth separating headline CPI from your personal inflation rate: CPI is a weighted basket meant to represent a typical household, but if your spending skews toward categories that have run hotter than average — rent in a supply-constrained metro, healthcare premiums, childcare, or tuition — your real erosion will run ahead of what the official number implies. Use the four time horizons to make different decisions: the 1-year and 5-year figures are useful for near-term budgeting and emergency-fund sizing, while the 10-year and 20-year figures are more relevant for retirement contribution rates and whether idle cash needs to be moved into inflation-resistant assets. None of this replaces a conversation with a financial advisor or tax professional about your specific situation, especially where the numbers touch retirement accounts, debt payoff tradeoffs, or major purchases.

faq.question: Why does the calculator show two separate erosion numbers instead of one?
faq.answer: Purchasing Power and Income Gap answer different questions. Purchasing Power tracks what your existing savings balance will actually buy in the future if it just sits there. Income Gap tracks whether your paycheck is keeping pace — it compares the income you'd need at year 10 to maintain today's lifestyle against what your stated annual raise rate actually delivers. A household can have healthy savings growth and still fall behind on Income Gap if raises consistently trail inflation, which is common in years when cost-of-living adjustments lag actual price increases.

faq.question: How is the $10,000-over-20-years example calculated step by step?
faq.answer: Start with Real Purchasing Power = Nominal Value ÷ (1 + Inflation Rate)^Years. Plug in $10,000, a 3% rate, and 20 years: (1.03)^20 ≈ 1.8061. Divide: 10,000 ÷ 1.8061 ≈ $5,537. That means $10,000 held in cash for 20 years under steady 3% inflation would need to grow to roughly $18,061 just to buy the same basket of goods it buys today — anything less than that growth rate represents a real loss, even if the account balance itself never went down.

faq.question: What is the Rule of 72 and how does it relate to this calculator?
faq.answer: The Rule of 72 is a shortcut for estimating doubling time: divide 72 by the annual rate to get approximate years to double. Applied to inflation, it estimates how long until prices double (and purchasing power roughly halves). At 2% inflation that's about 36 years; at 4% it's about 18 years; at 7% — closer to the pace seen during the 2021-2023 inflation spike — it's roughly 10 years. It's a mental-math approximation, not a substitute for the exact exponential formula this calculator uses, but it's a fast way to sanity-check whether a result looks plausible.

faq.question: Why does a small difference between my raise rate and inflation rate matter so much over time?
faq.answer: Because both are compounding rates working against each other, not simple annual differences. A 1-point gap sounds trivial in year one, but compounding stretches it out: a 2% raise against 4% inflation doesn't just cost you 2% of buying power each year, it costs a growing share of an already-shrunk base every year after that. Over 10 or 20 years that steady, unglamorous gap typically does more damage to a household's real standard of living than any single bad financial year, simply because it never lets up.

faq.question: Should I use official CPI or a higher personal inflation rate?
faq.answer: Official CPI is a broad, weighted average across a representative household's spending. If your own spending is concentrated in categories that have historically outpaced the headline number — housing in a tight rental market, healthcare premiums, childcare, or higher education — your realistic personal rate may run a point or two above CPI. Try running the calculator once at the current CPI figure and again at CPI plus 1-2 percentage points to see how sensitive your Income Gap and Total Erosion figures are to that assumption.

faq.question: Does the monthly savings contribution actually offset inflation erosion?
faq.answer: It offsets some of it, but the Total Wealth Erosion figure nets it against the discounting, not against the raw balance. Contributing $500 a month adds $6,000 a year in nominal terms, but that new money is also subject to the same real-value discount once it's been sitting for a while. Fresh contributions in year 19 haven't been eroded much yet; the original balance from year one has been eroding the whole time. The calculator's erosion figure reflects that blended effect rather than treating all dollars as equally aged.

faq.question: What can actually close the Income Gap or reduce Total Erosion?
faq.answer: Two levers exist: increase the growth rate of income (negotiated raises, job changes, additional income streams) or move idle savings into assets that have historically outpaced inflation over long periods — broad equity index funds, Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS), I-Bonds, or real estate. Holding a large cash cushion beyond what's needed for near-term expenses is the one strategy that guarantees erosion at whatever rate you enter, since cash by definition earns 0% nominal growth against a positive inflation rate.

faq.question: Why do the 1-year and 20-year numbers feel so different in magnitude?
faq.answer: Because erosion is exponential, not linear — it compounds the same way interest does, just working in the opposite direction. Going from year 1 to year 5 might shave off a few percentage points of purchasing power, but the damage per year accelerates as the eroded base itself keeps shrinking and compounding downward. That's why a 20-year projection often looks dramatically worse than four times the 5-year number: each additional year is discounting an already-smaller figure, the same mechanic that makes long-horizon compound growth look explosive in the other direction for investments.
